Title: I built a HOCON conformance suite. It found bugs in the reference implementation.
Description:
I have used HOCON in production for years. I like the format because it is readable and it allows config file composition, so it allows simple multi-environment config shared config files overrides minimizing config differences. As a Python developer, my ultimate combo for config management is Pydantic + pyhocon.
I like to try new things, so this June my eyes landed on Zig. I wanted to go back to the roots of programming and see what a modern “C” feels like. After reading the language reference I needed a project, and knowing the Java and Python implementations of HOCON don’t fully agree, it gave me an idea: “Zig has a native C interface, so why not write HOCON in Zig and expose it through C shim? Then every language can share one implementation. Magic!”
What a simple project I have picked, right?
Writing the tokenizer, the abstract syntax tree, the config and the resolution is the beautiful part. But right after the first implementation works, the question comes: am I really compatible? Luckily there is a written spec and a whole internet of examples. Well, it turned out the spec and the reference implementation do not always agree. Here is a basic config that contains an error:
hosts = [db1, db2] db3 The spec says an array next to a string in a concatenation is invalid. lightbend/config 1.4.9, the reference implementation, the one the spec was written for, gives you this:
{"hosts":["db1","db2"]} No error, no warning. db3 is gone. Write it the other way round, db3 [db1, db2], and you get the error you were promised.
So before going further with the parser, I wrote down what HOCON is supposed to do. That became a conformance suite: 445 cases, each one a sentence of the spec turned into a config file and the value it must produce. lightbend/config 1.4.9 passes 90% of them, pyhocon 70%. My Zig parser, zig-hocon, 69%, and from here on it is built against the suite.

Title: On Intelligence and Sentience
Description: I have a conjecture which I’m almost certain is true. Intelligence — as defined as ability to solve open-ended, novel problems — 1Yes it’s my em-dash if at all necessary, is not strictly the same as sentience, which — without defining it — consists of more than intelligence. Even if intelligence is a necessary ingredient for sentience (which I don’t think it is), sentience is a strict super set of it.

Title: GLM-Legal: Advancing Agentic Legal Intelligence
Description: Large language models are shifting from single-turn code generation toward broader professional collaboration (Professional Cowork). Real-world knowledge work introduces distinct requirements: models must digest fragmented source files under concrete objectives and tight delivery constraints, structure specialized knowledge into cohesive analysis, and maintain domain rigor across the full execution lifecycle. Legal work concentrates on these challenges, providing an ideal stress test for training models to operate in high-stakes professional environments.

Title: What's Wrong with GitHub - GNU Project
Description:
Software developers, the GNU Project urges you to avoid hosting your
repositories on GitHub. This is to avoid being on the receiving end of
harmful practices, and avoid leading others to be victims too. This article
focuses on a few of GitHub's worst problems, and the wrongs and harm they
can do:
(1) GitHub promotes vague and confusing
licensing practices;
(2) it demands that visitors run nonfree
JavaScript for most operations;
(3) some of the “services” it offers
are actually SaaSS (Service as a Software Substitute) dis-services;
(4) it attempts to subvert the
distributed architecture of Git.

Title: We spent $1200 on a booth at HITEX 2026. Here's what we got
Description:
I had a booth for Message24 at HITEX 2026, a tech expo run annually in Erbil where local companies and startups show their products to businesses and the public.
Message24 gives a business one inbox for all its social media messages, plus an AI agent that answers customers in multiple languages, so nobody is left waiting for a reply.
If you’re thinking about exhibiting at an expo like this, here is what we set out to do, what it cost, what worked and what we got.
